about.title: About Media Manipulator — A Free Online Media Converter, Editor & AI Toolkit
about.intro: Media Manipulator is a free online media converter, editor, transcriber, and metadata inspector for images, videos, and audio files. It is built and operated by CreaTV Ltd. and runs entirely on infrastructure we own — including a dedicated GPU server for AI features — so your files never leave systems we control.

mission.title: Our Mission
mission.p1: We started Media Manipulator because most "free media converter" sites are slow, upsell aggressively, paywall basic features behind sign-ups, send your files to third-party AI providers, or quietly retain uploads indefinitely. We wanted a free file converter online that you can trust: open in a browser, drop in a file, pick a setting, get a usable result. No account required, no software to install, no permanent storage of your media.
mission.p2: We treat conversion, editing, compression, transcription, summarization, and metadata management as one connected workflow rather than ten separate websites. If you want to compress an MP4 for the web, then trim it, generate VTT captions, and finally strip EXIF metadata from the thumbnail you'll publish alongside it — that's three different sites for most people and a single tab for Media Manipulator users.

whatItDoes.title: What Media Manipulator Does
whatItDoes.intro: Media Manipulator covers the full range of "I need to do something with this file" tasks across three media types. Everything runs on our servers — there is no desktop app to download, no Chrome extension to install, and no plug-in to update. Open the site, drop in a file, pick a tool, and download the result.

contentStudio.excerpt: A step-by-step guide to Darkroom — import media, build a multi-track timeline, trim, split and ripple-delete, add cross-dissolves, color adjustments and text overlays, then export MP4.

page.title: How to Use Darkroom
page.intro: Darkroom is a Premiere Pro–style, multi-track video editor that runs entirely in your browser. Upload video, images, and audio, arrange them on a timeline, layer and mix tracks, add effects, and export a finished MP4 — no software to install. This guide walks through the whole workflow.
page.overviewAlt: The Darkroom editor showing the media bin, preview, clip effects panel, and a multi-track timeline.
page.overviewCaption: The Darkroom workspace: media bin (left), live preview (center), clip effects (right), and the multi-track timeline (bottom).

create.title: 1. Create a project
create.body: Open Darkroom from the Tools page or the home page banner, then choose “New project”. Pick a name, a target resolution (1080p, 720p, 4K, or vertical 1080×1920) and a frame rate (24, 30, or 60 fps). These define the canvas your timeline renders to on export. Your recent projects appear next to the form so you can jump back into earlier edits.

media.title: 2. Add your media
media.body: Drag video, image, or audio files into the Media box, or click “Choose files”. Each upload is analyzed and given a smooth 720p preview proxy plus a filmstrip — you’ll see a brief “building preview” state while that happens. Video (mp4, mov, webm, mkv, …), images (jpg, png, webp, heic, avif, gif, bmp, tiff), and audio (mp3, wav, m4a, aac, ogg, flac) are all supported — images are held as stills you can stretch to any length — and you can add as many files as you like.

timeline.title: 3. Build your timeline
timeline.body: Put clips on the timeline either by clicking the + on a media tile (it’s appended to the first matching track) or by dragging a media tile straight onto the track you want. From there you can rearrange everything:

bullets.tracks: Add more tracks with the +V / +A buttons — stack multiple video tracks for overlays and multiple audio tracks for music and voiceover.
bullets.drag: Drag a clip along its track to reposition it, or drop it onto another track of the same kind (video→video, audio→audio). Clips snap to neighbouring edges and the playhead and never overlap.
bullets.trim: Drag either edge of a clip to trim its in/out point.
bullets.split: Move the playhead and press Cmd/Ctrl+K to split (razor) the clip(s) under it.
bullets.ripple: Select a clip and use Ripple delete to remove it and close the gap. Mute a whole track with the speaker icon, or set a clip’s volume with the slider.

effects.title: 4. Add effects
effects.body: Select a single clip to open the Clip effects panel on the right. From there you can apply a cross-dissolve, color adjustments, and text/location overlays — all previewed live and baked into the final export.

color.title: Color adjustments
color.body: Click “Adjust” under Color, then tune Brightness, Contrast, and Saturation. The preview updates instantly (for example, drop saturation to zero for a black-and-white look). “Reset” removes the adjustment.

text.title: Text & location overlays
text.body: Click “Add text” to drop a label onto the clip — type your text, pick a color, and position it with the X/Y sliders and size it to taste. Overlays are great for titles or location labels over drone footage and are drawn directly into the exported video.

dissolve.title: Cross-dissolves
dissolve.body: With a clip that has another clip before it on the same track selected, drag the Cross-dissolve slider — the clip slides back to overlap its neighbour and the two blend over that duration, with the audio crossfading to match.

page.effectsAlt: The Clip effects panel with cross-dissolve, color, and text overlay controls for the selected clip.
page.effectsCaption: Selecting a clip reveals the Clip effects panel: cross-dissolve, color, and text overlays.
page.colorAlt: Color adjustment sliders for brightness, contrast, and saturation, with the preview desaturated.
page.colorCaption: Brightness / Contrast / Saturation update the preview live — here saturation is pulled down for a black-and-white look.
page.textAlt: A red “This is my video!” text overlay drawn over the preview with the text editor on the right.
page.textCaption: Text overlays are positioned and styled in the panel and drawn into the preview and the export.

preview.title: 5. Preview your edit
preview.body: Use the transport controls under the preview to play/pause, step a frame at a time, or jump to the start/end. Drag on the timeline ruler to scrub — drag to the edge and the timeline auto-scrolls so you can reach any point. During playback the view follows the playhead automatically.

export.title: 6. Export to MP4
export.body: Click “Export MP4”, choose a file name and quality, and Darkroom renders your full timeline on the server — compositing video tracks, mixing audio, and applying your effects — then gives you a download link. Rendering happens on a GPU, so larger projects finish quickly.

shortcuts.title: Keyboard shortcuts
shortcuts.body: Space play/pause · ← / → step one frame · S split at playhead · Delete ripple-delete the selection · + / − zoom the timeline.

motion.title: How to Animate an SVG with Motion
motion.excerpt: A five-step guide to Motion: import an SVG, animate it with keyframes, shape the timing with easing and holds, export it, and choose the right format.

page.title: How to animate an SVG with {{brand}}
page.intro: {{brand}} turns a static SVG into an animation without writing code. You work with layers and a keyframe timeline, like a motion design app, and export the result as an animated SVG, a Lottie file, a React component, a JavaScript or TypeScript module, a Flutter widget or a GIF. This guide goes from an empty canvas to a finished export in five steps.

import.title: 1. Import an SVG or start from scratch
import.body: Open {{brand}} from its tool page. The editor opens full screen with a blank 512 × 512 canvas. Choose Import to bring in your artwork, or draw directly on the canvas.

bullets.svg: SVG files become a layer tree: groups, paths, rectangles, ellipses, lines, polygons, text, images, gradients, masks and clip paths are all editable. Select a layer in the Layers panel or on the canvas, and rename, group, lock or hide it.
bullets.lottie: Lottie JSON files are imported with their keyframes, so you can edit an existing animation. Anything the editor cannot represent is listed after the import instead of being dropped silently.
bullets.blank: To draw from scratch, use the Rectangle, Ellipse, Line, Pen and Text tools. Edit nodes lets you reshape any path point by point.
bullets.safety: Imports are cleaned on the way in: scripts, event handlers and links to outside files are removed and listed, so an SVG from the web cannot run code in the editor or in your exports.

animate.title: 2. Animate with keyframes
animate.body: The timeline at the bottom of the editor shows one row per layer and one track per animated property. {{brand}} uses the playhead to decide where a change goes.

bullets.playhead: Drag the playhead (or click the time ruler) to the moment the change should happen. Space plays and pauses, Home and End jump to the start and end.
bullets.keyframe: With a layer selected, use Animate on a property in the inspector to give it a track, then change the value. Each change at a new time adds a keyframe; changing an animated property later edits the keyframe at the playhead.
bullets.autokey: Turn on Auto-key to record every change you make on the canvas or in the inspector as a keyframe, which is fastest for rough blocking.
bullets.animators: The Animate panel adds whole effects in one step: Draw on (the stroke draws itself), Motion path (the layer travels along a path), Morph (one shape becomes another), Gradient, Mask/Clip and Blur. Each one is a single undo step.

easing.title: 3. Shape the timing with easing and holds
easing.body: Easing decides how a value travels between two keyframes. Select one or more keyframes on the timeline and pick an easing in the Easing panel; it applies to the segment that starts at each selected keyframe.

bullets.presets: Linear, Ease in, Ease out and Ease in-out cover most motion. Ease out suits things arriving; ease in suits things leaving.
bullets.curve: Curve opens a cubic-bezier editor with two handles, for overshoot-free custom timing that matches CSS cubic-bezier() exactly.
bullets.hold: Hold keeps the value unchanged until the next keyframe, then jumps. Use it for blinking, frame-by-frame swaps or a colour that changes instantly.
bullets.range: Set a play range to loop just the part you are working on, and turn Loop off if the animation should play once.

export.title: 4. Export your animation
export.body: Choose Export to open the export dialog. Every export is made in your browser and downloaded straight away; your artwork is not uploaded. Static SVG (the frame at the playhead) is always free. Animated formats count toward your plan's daily {{brand}} allowance, which the dialog shows before you export, and formats your plan does not include are marked with a lock and a link to the plans.

formats.title: 5. Pick the right format
formats.body: The best format depends on where the animation will play.

bullets.svg: Animated SVG is one file that plays without any library, ideal for websites. It uses pure CSS when it can; shape morphs, moving gradient stops and blur need a small embedded script (anime.js, MIT licence), and scripts do not run when the SVG is placed in an tag.
bullets.lottie: Lottie JSON plays in lottie-web and the iOS, Android and Flutter Lottie players. The dialog lists anything Lottie cannot carry, such as filters or text.
bullets.code: React (.tsx), JavaScript and TypeScript exports give you a component or module with play, pause and seek, ready to drop into an app.
bullets.flutter: The Flutter export is a native flutter_svg widget when the animation only moves, fades and recolours, and a WebView player for everything else.
bullets.gif: GIF plays everywhere, including chat and email, with one global palette that keeps flat vector colours exact. GIF and video exports follow your plan's size and length limits.

save.body: {{brand}} saves a draft in this browser as you work, so a closed tab or a crash does not lose your changes. Without an account, projects live only in this browser. When you are signed in, Save to account stores the project on our servers; after that it autosaves, opens on any device and appears on your Account page, where you can delete it.

page.title: How to edit a photo with {{brand}}
page.intro: {{brand}} is Media Manipulator's non-destructive photo editor. Every change you make is an adjustment layer stacked over the untouched original, so you can reorder, mask, fade or delete any step later, and the file you opened is never altered. The preview is drawn on your graphics card from a 1920 px copy; the export is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same formulas. This guide walks through one edit from opening a photo to applying the finished look to a whole set, using the panel and slider names you will see in the editor.

open.title: 1. Open a photo
open.body: Open {{brand}} from its tool page or from any photo tool page on Media Manipulator. The editor takes over the whole screen with no ads. Drop a photo onto the open screen or press Choose a photo. Once it is decoded you get the preview in the middle, the Panels and Layers tabs on one side, and a live histogram showing red, green, blue and luminance. Hold the backslash key at any time to see the original, or turn on Split view to compare halves.

bullets.formats: You can open JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF and BMP files. Your browser decodes the common web formats on its own. HEIC, HEIF, TIFF and BMP need an account, because the server makes a preview copy before the editor can show them.
bullets.local: Without an account, the photo and your edits stay in this browser's storage and nothing is uploaded until you export, select a subject or heal. Guests keep one photo at a time; opening a second one replaces the saved project, and the editor asks before it does so.
bullets.account: Signed in, each photo becomes a project saved to your account: 5 projects on Free, 50 on Premium and unlimited on Pro. The project opens on any device and autosaves as you work, with the saved state shown in the top bar.
bullets.original: The original file is never changed. Every adjustment is a layer over it, with its own opacity from 0 to 100 percent, a blend mode of normal, luminosity or color, and an optional mask. You can stack up to 64 layers, and the History panel lists every step.

basic.title: 2. Fix light and color with Basic
basic.body: Most photos need the Basic panel first. It groups the global sliders into Exposure, Light, Tone, White balance and Color sections, each of which becomes its own adjustment layer the moment you move a slider. Work from the top down: get overall brightness right, then recover highlights and shadows, then correct the color cast, then decide how much color you want. Watch the histogram while you drag; clipping shows up as a pile-up at either end.

bullets.exposure: Exposure (EV) runs from -5 to +5 stops and multiplies every pixel by two to the power of the value, so +1 doubles the light. Offset adds or subtracts a flat amount from -0.5 to 0.5, and Gamma from 0.1 to 10 bends the midtones. Light holds Brightness and Contrast from -100 to 100.
bullets.tone: Tone has Highlights, Shadows, Whites and Blacks. Pull Highlights down to bring back a bright sky, raise Shadows to open a dark face, and use Whites and Blacks to set where the brightest and darkest points land. Each slider targets its own part of the luminance range instead of moving everything.
bullets.whiteBalance: White balance has Temperature and Tint. Temperature shifts the photo toward blue or amber; Tint shifts it toward green or magenta. Indoor shots under warm bulbs usually need Temperature pulled toward blue, and fluorescent light often needs a little magenta Tint. Judge the result on something that should be neutral gray or white.
bullets.history: Nothing here is permanent. Undo and redo are on the top bar and the keyboard, the History panel jumps back to any earlier state, and you can save a named snapshot of a version you like for the rest of the session. Lower a layer's opacity to apply half of an adjustment instead of redoing it.

colorPop.title: 3. Make one color pop
colorPop.body: The selective color effect, where one color stays and everything else turns gray, lives in the Color (HSL) panel. You can get there in one step with a built-in look or build it by hand. The hand-built route gives you control over exactly which hues survive and how soft the edge between color and gray is, which matters for things like skin that sits between reds and yellows.

bullets.look: In the Looks panel, choose Color pop: red, yellow, green, cyan, blue or magenta. The look adds a Color (HSL) layer on top of your edits that desaturates every range except the one you picked. If it is not what you wanted, a single Undo removes the whole look.
bullets.chips: To build it yourself, open Color (HSL). Each of the six ranges, Reds, Yellows, Greens, Cyans, Blues and Magentas, has a Gray except this chip. Press the chip on the color you want to keep and the other five ranges drop to minus 100 saturation in one move.
bullets.ranges: If the color you want to keep is not one of the six, use Pick a color from the photo to add a custom range with the eyedropper. Each range has Width and Feather controls, so you can widen it to include neighboring hues or soften the border so the transition does not look cut out.
bullets.tune: Then fine-tune the surviving color with its own Hue, Saturation and Lightness sliders. A little extra Saturation and a touch less Lightness usually makes the kept color read stronger against gray. If the look is too strong overall, lower the layer's opacity in the Layers tab rather than redoing it.

masks.title: 4. Edit only part of the photo with masks
masks.body: Any adjustment layer can carry a mask, which limits where it applies. Select the layer in the Layers tab, open Masks and add a component. White areas of the mask get the full adjustment, black areas get none, and gray areas get a proportion. Mask view switches between off, a colored overlay on the photo and the mask alone, so you can see exactly what you are affecting before you start moving sliders.

bullets.kinds: There are six mask kinds: Linear gradient for a sky or a floor, Radial for a spotlight around a point, Brush for painting by hand with adjustable size and an erase toggle, Luminosity range for the bright or dark parts only, Color range for pixels of a chosen color, and Select subject.
bullets.combine: A mask can hold several components, and each one is set to Add, Subtract or Intersect. A common recipe is a Linear gradient over the sky with a Subtract Brush that protects a building that pokes into it. Mask feather softens the edge, Mask strength scales the whole thing, and Invert flips it.
bullets.colorRange: Color range uses the same eyedropper idea as the HSL panel: pick a color, shift-click to add up to eight more, and raise Fuzziness to include nearby shades. It is a quick way to darken only a blue sky or warm only the skin tones without painting anything.
bullets.subject: Select subject asks our GPU to find the main person or object and returns a soft-edged mask in a few seconds. It is the one mask kind that uploads the photo and counts as an everyday operation on your plan; an identical repeat is a free cache hit. Every other mask kind is computed in your browser and costs nothing.

heal.title: 5. Heal spots and blemishes
heal.body: Dust on a sensor, a pimple, a stray wire or a bit of litter can all go through the Heal panel. Unlike the sliders, healing is a generative step: our server fills the painted area with new pixels that match the surroundings. It still lands in your layer stack and your history, so you can undo it or hold backslash to compare with the original, but it is the one tool in this guide that costs an AI operation.

bullets.paint: Pick the Spot brush and paint over each mark you want gone. Make the dab a little larger than the spot itself so the fill has clean texture to blend into. The panel counts the spots you have marked, and Clear spots starts over if you change your mind before pressing Heal.
bullets.press: Press Heal when the spots are marked. The photo and the painted area go to our GPU, where the LaMa inpainting model fills the marked areas; this can take up to a minute on a large file. When it comes back, the result is applied as a step in your history with an Undo available.
bullets.cost: Each press of Heal is one AI operation on your plan, no matter how many spots you painted, so mark everything first and press once. The daily allowance per plan is listed on the pricing page. Painting spots, clearing them and undoing a heal cost nothing.
bullets.base: Healing sits in your layer stack like everything else, so the color and tone layers you add afterward apply to the healed result, and Undo or the History panel takes it back out. For red eyes in flash portraits there is a separate Red-eye panel that needs no AI at all.

export.title: 6. Export at full resolution
export.body: Press Export on the top bar when the edit is finished. The preview you have been working on is a 1920 px copy drawn on your graphics card; the export is a server job that renders the original at its full size with the same formulas, so the two agree to within a few 8-bit levels at most. The result is downloaded as a new file named after the original with (retouched) added, and the original file is untouched.

bullets.format: Choose JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF, set Quality from 1 to 100 where it applies, and choose whether to Keep or Strip the metadata. Stripping removes the EXIF block, including camera settings and any GPS location, which is usually what you want before posting a photo publicly.
bullets.size: Max size offers Original, 12, 24, 64 and 120 megapixels. The dialog estimates the file size for your choice: a JPG at quality 92 is about 0.45 MB per megapixel, so a 6000 x 4000 photo at 24 MP comes out near 10.8 MB, while WebP is around 0.3 MB and AVIF around 0.2 MB per megapixel.
bullets.server: Exports up to 12 MP are available to guests and on the Free plan, so a larger original is exported at 12 MP. Premium and Pro export up to 120 MP. The job runs on our server, which renders with NumPy and OpenCV, encodes with ImageMagick and offers the file for download when it is done.
bullets.cost: One export is one everyday operation on your plan, and you can run Export again with different settings afterward, for example a full-size TIFF for printing and a 12 MP WebP for the web. Previewing, every slider, every non-AI mask, looks and undo are free and unlimited.

presets.title: 7. Save and reuse looks
presets.body: A look in {{brand}} is a saved group of adjustment layers. The Looks panel ships with 18 built-in looks plus Auto, and it is also where your own presets live. Saving a preset captures the layers you choose with their current values, so the warm, slightly faded treatment you dialed in for one photo can be dropped onto the next one in a single click, and still comes in as editable layers rather than a baked-in filter.

bullets.builtin: The built-in looks are grouped as Color, Black & white, Film and Fix, and include the six Color pop looks, Black & white film, High-contrast black & white, Warm, Cool, Matte, Fade, Vivid, Punch, Cross-process, Vintage, Portrait soften, Landscape and Auto. Use the filter box to find one by name.
bullets.append: Applying a look adds its adjustments as a named group on top of what you already have instead of replacing your work. That means you can stack Warm over your own Basic corrections, open the group in the Layers tab to tweak individual sliders, and remove the whole look with one Undo.
bullets.mine: Choose Save current edits as a preset, give it a name and tick the adjustments to include. It appears under My presets. When you are signed in your presets are stored on your account and follow you to your other devices; without an account they are stored in this browser. You can rename or delete them from the same panel.
bullets.file: Export presets writes your saved presets to a JSON file; Import presets reads one back in. Use this to move presets to another browser or computer, to keep a backup, or to share a look with someone else who uses {{brand}} on Media Manipulator.

batch.title: 8. Apply the same edits to more photos
batch.body: When several photos from the same shoot need the same treatment, you do not have to repeat the edit. Finish one photo, open the Export dialog and choose Apply to more photos. It takes the entire layer stack of the current project, including masks and healing you have already done on this photo, and renders it onto the other files you pick with the export settings you chose, then hands you everything as one download.

bullets.limit: Apply to more photos is available only when you are signed in; the dialog asks guests to sign in. The Free plan applies edits to up to 3 photos at a time, Premium up to 10 and Pro up to 25. Pick more than your plan allows and the extra files are left out, and the dialog says how many.
bullets.run: Each chosen photo is first created as its own project in your account, one after another, so the originals and their edits are kept like any other project. Then a single batch job renders them all on the server, and the dialog shows each photo move from Preparing to Rendering with a percentage to Done.
bullets.zip: When the renders finish, press Download as ZIP. The archive is built in your browser from the finished files, so nothing extra is uploaded and you get one file to save instead of a dozen separate downloads. If a file could not be added, the dialog tells you how many are missing.
bullets.retry: If a photo fails, the others are not held up. The dialog shows how many failed and offers a Retry button for just those files, and the ZIP can be built again once they finish. Exports count as everyday operations on your plan, so check the pricing page before running a large batch.

page.intro: {{brand}} is the assistant inside Media Manipulator: a guide on every public page and a copilot in Aperture, Darkroom and Motion. This tutorial covers three workflows, in the order most people need them. In all of them {{brand}} only prepares or proposes; you press the button.

find.title: 1. Find the right tool
find.body: Press the {{brand}} button in the corner of any public page and describe the result you want in your own words, in any language the site supports. {{brand}} answers from the site's own help pages and names the tool, the one setting that matters, and a link.

bullets.ask: Say the goal, not the tool: for example, make this video small enough to email.
bullets.attach: Use the paperclip to attach a file. {{brand}} reads its type, size, duration and codecs so the advice fits that file.
bullets.scope: It only talks about Media Manipulator and will decline anything else.
bullets.plans: Questions about plans are answered from the live plan table, never from memory.

job.title: 2. Let {{brand}} prepare a job
job.body: Say what you want done, or drop a file and say just run it. {{brand}} shows a confirmation card: the settings in your language, how long the queue is and which daily allowance the job would use. Nothing has started.

bullets.card: Read the settings. They are checked against the tool's real options, so an unsupported value is refused instead of changed.
bullets.start: Start runs in place for video compress, resize, rotate, crop and trim, audio extract and remove, and transcription; the result opens in a window.
bullets.open: Every other tool opens on its own page with the settings filled in, and you press its button there.
bullets.click: A click is always required. Medi never starts anything by itself.

edit.title: 3. Edit by describing the result
edit.body: In Aperture, Darkroom or Motion, sign in and press Ctrl+J, then describe the look or change you want. {{brand}} edits the project as a single step and gives a reason for every change.

bullets.undo: Undo takes the whole edit back in one step.
bullets.review: Switch off automatic application in the information menu to review each edit as a card with Apply and Discard first.
bullets.showMe: Show me opens the control an edit changed so you can see and learn it.
bullets.numbers: {{brand}} can measure the preview, such as brightness, clipped shadows or loudness, and adjust up to three times, citing the figure each time.

privacyPolicy.title: Privacy Policy
privacyPolicy.intro: Media Manipulator is owned and operated by CreaTV Ltd. (“CreaTV,” “Media Manipulator,” “we,” “us,” or “our”). Media Manipulator provides browser-based and server-assisted tools for editing, converting, compressing, analyzing, transcribing, summarizing, and otherwise processing image, video, and audio files.
privacyPolicy.blockquote: Where Media Manipulator uses AI-assisted features, those AI systems run locally on our own servers or infrastructure that we control and are not outsourced to third-party AI providers.
privacyPolicy.explanation: This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, store, protect, and delete information when you use our website, tools, and related services.
privacyPolicy.acceptance: By using Media Manipulator, you agree to the practices described in this Privacy Policy.

sections.title: 1. Information We Collect
paragraphs: We collect information in several ways depending on how you use the website.

subsections.title: 1.1 Files You Upload
paragraphs: When you upload an image, video, audio file, or other supported media file to Media Manipulator, we may temporarily process that file to provide the requested tool functionality, such as:
bullets: converting a file to another format;
cropping, trimming, resizing, compressing, filtering, or editing media;
extracting or displaying metadata;
removing metadata;
generating transcripts, captions, summaries, descriptions, or other AI-assisted outputs;
creating downloadable processed files;
keeping your conversion history so you can download or reopen recent conversions.
afterBullets: Uploaded files and generated outputs are kept for the retention period described in Section 3: 24 hours if you do not have an account, or the period you choose if you are signed in. You can delete them sooner.

If you use the metadata inspector, the file is analyzed on our server with ExifTool and ffprobe, the report is returned to your browser, and the temporary copy of the uploaded file is deleted as soon as the analysis finishes.

subsections.title: 1.2 File and Conversion Metadata
paragraphs: We may collect technical information about uploaded files and conversion jobs, including:
bullets: file name;
file type or MIME type;
file size;
file duration, dimensions, bitrate, codec, or other technical properties;
conversion settings selected by the user;
generated output format;
job status, processing errors, and timestamps;
temporary file identifiers or session identifiers.
afterBullets: We use this information to operate the service, troubleshoot failed conversions, maintain temporary session history, improve performance, detect abuse, and protect the website.

subsections.title: 1.3 Content Scanning and Safety Review
paragraphs: All uploads may be subject to automated scanning and classification for security, abuse prevention, brand safety, advertiser protection, and detection or blocking of suspected illegal or prohibited content.
These scans may be used to identify or help prevent content involving, for example:
bullets: suspected child sexual abuse material or exploitation;
malware, malicious files, or harmful code;
content that appears to violate applicable law;
content that violates our Terms of Service or Acceptable Use rules;
adult, sexually explicit, graphic, violent, or otherwise advertiser-sensitive content.
afterBullets: If content is determined or suspected to be illegal, prohibited, abusive, or unsafe, we may block processing, delete the file, prevent display of previews, restrict access to generated outputs, preserve limited records where legally required, or report the content to appropriate authorities if required by law.

If content is lawful but classified as adult, graphic, violent, or otherwise advertiser-sensitive, we may prevent that content from being displayed or previewed on the website in order to protect users, our brand, and advertisers. In some cases, where lawful and technically available, the user may still be able to download the processed file.
Users are solely responsible for the files they upload and for ensuring they have all rights, permissions, and legal authority necessary to process those files using Media Manipulator.

subsections.title: 1.4 Usage Data
paragraphs: When you visit or use Media Manipulator, we may automatically collect usage and device information, such as:
bullets: pages visited;
tools used;
buttons clicked;
approximate location based on IP address;
browser type and version;
operating system;
device type;
referral source;
timestamps;
diagnostic logs;
error logs;
performance data;
analytics events.
afterBullets: We use this information to understand how users use the website, improve features, diagnose issues, prevent abuse, and measure website performance.

subsections.title: 1.5 Cookies and Similar Technologies
paragraphs: We and our service providers may use cookies, local storage, pixels, tags, and similar technologies to:
bullets: operate the website;
remember user preferences;
maintain session functionality;
analyze traffic and usage;
detect abuse or security risks;
serve and measure advertisements.
afterBullets: You can control cookies through your browser settings. Some features may not work properly if cookies or local storage are disabled.

Advertising identifiers set by Google’s ad script: when ads are switched on, Google’s script may store identifiers in your browser, which Google documents as the first-party cookies __gads and __gpi on our domain (kept for up to 13 months), Google’s own cookies such as IDE on doubleclick.net (13 months in the EEA, the UK and Switzerland, 24 months elsewhere), and similar entries in local storage. Google uses them to serve and measure ads, to limit how often you see the same ad, to prevent ad fraud and, only if you allow it, to personalise ads. How long each one is kept is set by Google’s policy: https://policies.google.com/technologies/cookies. They are set only when ads are on and you have allowed advertising storage; in the EEA, the UK and Switzerland, that means only after you consent in Google’s consent message. See Section 5.1.

subsections.title: 1.6 Payment and Subscription Data
paragraphs: If you subscribe to Premium or Pro, payment is handled by our payment processor, Stripe. Your card details are entered on Stripe's pages and are processed by Stripe; we do not receive or store card numbers.

We store only what we need to run your subscription: your Stripe customer identifier, your subscription status, your plan (Premium or Pro), your billing interval (monthly or yearly), the currency you are billed in (US dollars or euros), and the date your current period ends. A plan change you schedule (for example from Pro to Premium at the end of the period) is kept by Stripe, and we read it from Stripe to show it on your Account page. We use this information to give you the right plan, show your billing status, and handle refunds and support requests. If you choose a currency on the pricing page, we remember it in a cookie named mm-currency and in your browser's local storage, and, if you are signed in, in your account settings; it holds only “usd” or “eur”.

Our Stripe account belongs to CreaTV Ltd., the company that operates Media Manipulator. As a result, Stripe's checkout page shows CreaTV (or CreaTV Ltd.) branding instead of Media Manipulator. The charge on your card statement appears as “MEDIA MNPLTR PREMIUM”.

subsections.title: 1.7 Account Information
paragraphs: If you create an account, sign-in is handled by Firebase Authentication, a Google service. You can sign in with an email address and password, with your Google account or with your Apple Account. If you sign in with Apple, Apple shares your name and email address with us, or, if you choose "Hide My Email", a private relay address that forwards to you; Apple's privacy policy applies to your Apple Account. Firebase stores your credentials and sends the emails it needs to run sign-in, such as email verification. If you ask to reset your password, Firebase sends a reset link to your email address.

On our side we store a record for your account: your email address, display name, whether your email is verified, your Firebase sign-in identifier, your plan, when you signed up and last used the service, the retention settings you chose, and your conversion history and projects (Section 3). We send a small number of service emails from Media Manipulator: a welcome email, payment and account-deletion notices, and, if you keep them switched on in your account settings, reminders before your files expire and notices when a long AI job finishes. We do not send marketing email. Emails are delivered through our email provider, Resend.

subsections.title: 1.8 Darkroom Inside CreaTV Studio
paragraphs: Darkroom, our video editor, can also be embedded inside CreaTV Studio, a product of the same company. In that mode, CreaTV Studio passes your CreaTV sign-in token to the embedded editor through your browser (a message between the CreaTV page and the editor), and the editor uses it only to call CreaTV's own studio services. Your projects, media and exports are then stored and processed by CreaTV's services under your CreaTV account, not in a Media Manipulator account, and CreaTV's own privacy policy applies to them.

CreaTV Studio also tells the embedded editor whether you have accepted analytics and advertising on CreaTV. The embedded editor does not show our cookie banner or ads, and it does not run our analytics.

subsections.title: 1.9 Motion Projects and Exports
paragraphs: Motion, our SVG animation editor, runs in your browser. The drawings you import or create and the files you export from them (animated SVG, Lottie, code, GIF and other formats) are produced in your browser. We do not receive your artwork or the exported files to make them.

Without an account, Motion projects are kept only in your browser (in IndexedDB) and never reach our servers. If you are signed in and choose “Save to account”, the project and a small thumbnail image are stored on our servers and in Amazon S3 in the same way as a Darkroom project: they are your content, they follow the retention period you choose (Section 3), you can delete them from your Account page, they are deleted with your account, and they are listed in your data export.

Each animated export and each Lottie import is counted on our server before your browser runs it, to enforce your plan's daily Motion allowance. For each one we store the format, the output height, frame rate and length, the time, your plan, the saved project it came from (if any), and an identifier for your account, your browser session or a hashed IP address. We use these records to enforce the allowance and to understand which formats are used. When you delete your account, they are detached from your identity.

subsections.title: 1.10 Voice Samples and Designed Voices
paragraphs: When you use the voice tools, we process the voice recordings you record or upload, the voices you save, and the text you ask a voice to speak (used only to generate that speech). A saved voice consists of its name, its kind (cloned from a recording, or designed from a description), its language, for a designed voice the description and the seed used to generate it, a reference recording (your recording, or for a designed voice a 10-second clip we render), a short preview, the version of the voice engine and, for a cloned voice, the time you confirmed your consent and the version of the consent text.

Purpose and legal basis: we use these data only to create and run the voice you asked for, that is, to make the voice, render its preview, and generate or convert speech when you ask. A recording of a person's voice can identify them, so we treat it with the care that special-category (biometric) data requires and rely on your explicit consent, which you give with the consent checkbox before a voice is created from a recording. You can withdraw it at any time by deleting the voice.

Storage: saved voices are stored on our servers and in Amazon S3 under voices/, in your account, and follow the retention period you choose (Section 3). Recordings you upload to change and the speech you generate are kept like any other upload and result. Voice processing runs on our own GPU server: your recordings and voices are never shared with a third-party AI provider and are never used to train any model. Generated and converted speech carries an inaudible watermark that marks it as synthetic; it contains no account details.

Deletion and export: you can delete a saved voice at any time from Account, Voices; its reference recording and preview are deleted from our servers straight away, while speech you already generated stays until its own retention period ends. All your saved voices are deleted when you delete your account. Your data export lists your saved voices (name, kind, language, dates and the consent record), without the audio.

subsections.title: 1.11 Messages You Send Us
paragraphs: When you use the contact form at media-manipulator.com/contact, we receive your name, your email address, the subject you choose and your message, together with the time it was sent and a short reference number. The form delivers this to our support mailbox by email, through our email provider Resend; contact messages are not stored in our application database. When you email us directly, we receive the same kind of information from your email.

We use these messages only to answer you and to handle what you ask for, such as a bug report, a billing question or a privacy request. They are kept in our support mailbox until the conversation is closed, and never longer than 12 months. To limit spam, the form is rate-limited per browser session and per IP address like the rest of the site, and a blocked attempt is kept as an abuse-prevention record (Section 3.6).

subsections.title: 1.12 Aperture Projects and Exports
paragraphs: Aperture, our photo editor, edits your photo in your browser: the preview you see is drawn on your own device. A photo leaves your device only when you ask for something that needs our servers: saving it to your account as a project, exporting the finished file, selecting a subject with AI, healing spots with AI, or applying your edits to more photos.

If you are signed in and save a project, the original photo, a preview copy of it at up to 1920 pixels, a small thumbnail, the editing document (the list of adjustments, masks and healed areas) and any masks and healed versions of the photo are stored on our servers in the project's folder. They are your content, they follow the retention period you choose (Section 3), you can delete a project from your Account page, they are deleted with your account, and the projects are listed in your data export. Without an account, one photo is kept only in your browser (in IndexedDB) and is not uploaded until you export, select a subject or heal; that upload is a normal temporary job and is kept for 24 hours. Presets you save are stored with your account until you delete them or the account.

Exports, AI subject selection and healing are jobs on our servers. Exports are rendered from your original photo, subject selection and healing run on our own GPU server, and none of your photos is sent to a third-party service. Each export, subject selection and healing is counted to enforce your plan's daily allowance: we store the kind of job, the format and size of the result, the time, your plan and an identifier for your account, your browser session or a hashed IP address. The result files are kept under the usual retention rules (Section 3), and when you delete your account these records are detached from your identity.

subsections.title: 1.13 Medi, the AI Assistant
paragraphs: Medi is our AI assistant: a guide to the site that anyone can ask, and an editing assistant in our editors for signed-in users. To answer you, Medi sends what you type to OpenRouter, Inc., which passes it to Anthropic, the company that makes the Claude models Medi uses. Your message travels with the page you are on, the help pages that match your question, your plan and your remaining Medi allowance. In the editors it also travels with a short text summary of your open project (for example its layer, clip or track names and settings) and, when an edit needs it, a small preview image of your work (at most 1024 pixels). Medi does not send your original files.

We configure every Medi request to go only to Anthropic, with no fallback to other providers, and with OpenRouter's data policy setting that excludes providers that collect user data. OpenRouter states that it does not use your inputs or outputs to train models. Anthropic states that by default it does not use inputs and outputs of its commercial products to train models and deletes them within 30 days, except where it keeps them longer for legal reasons or to enforce its usage policies. Their own privacy policies apply to what they receive.

If you are signed in, we store your Medi conversations (your messages, Medi's answers and short summaries of the edits it made) so you can see them again. They follow the retention period you choose (Section 3), you can delete a conversation at any time, they are included in your data export and they are deleted with your account. If you are not signed in, we do not store your conversation. Preview images are never stored by us, in conversations, logs or analytics. For every answer, signed in or not, we keep a usage record with no text: the time, the part of the site, the model, the number of tokens, the cost, your account if you are signed in and a one-way hash of your browser identifier, kept for 13 months to enforce the daily allowance and our spending limit. If you rate an answer, we store your rating with that message.
Medi's answers are generated by AI and can be wrong. Check an answer before you rely on it, and review edits before you publish your work.

sections.title: 2. How We Use Information
paragraphs: We use the information we collect to:
bullets: provide media conversion, editing, transcription, metadata, AI analysis, and related tools;
store your conversion history for the retention period that applies to you (24 hours for visitors without an account, or the period you choose if you are signed in);
allow users to download recent converted files while they are retained;
scan uploads for suspected illegal, prohibited, abusive, or advertiser-sensitive content;
protect users, advertisers, our website, and our brand;
prevent fraud, abuse, spam, malware, and security incidents;
debug errors and improve service reliability;
analyze traffic and usage trends;
improve our website, tools, user experience, and performance;
comply with legal obligations;
enforce our Terms of Service and Acceptable Use rules.

sections.title: 3. File Storage, Retention and Deletion
paragraphs: How long we keep your files depends on whether you have an account. This section covers uploaded files, generated outputs (results), Darkroom media, Darkroom projects, Motion projects, Aperture projects and saved voices in your account, stored on our servers and in Amazon S3 (us-west-2). Records about your conversions and settings (such as job history, retention choices and account details) are kept in a PostgreSQL database, and AI processing runs on our own self-hosted GPU server.

subsections.title: 3.1 How long we keep your files
bullets: Visitors without an account: files are kept for 24 hours.
Signed-in users: you choose a retention period from 24 hours to 2 years. Every account has this choice; it does not depend on your plan. Until you choose, the default is 6 months.
afterBullets: The period is counted from when each file or project was created. When you change the period it also applies to your existing files, measured from their creation date, so choosing a shorter period can cause existing files to be deleted soon afterwards. You can keep an individual result longer from your History.
If you sign in after using the service as a visitor, files from that visit may be attached to your account and then follow your chosen period.

Expired files are removed by an automated cleanup that runs regularly, so deletion may happen a short time after the period ends. After deletion, files are no longer available in our active systems. We keep no backups of media.

Recent history on this device: for visitors without an account, the Recent list on the home and tool pages is stored in this browser only (in IndexedDB). It holds the job ID, tool, result file name, size, timing and a small thumbnail, never the file itself. It is not sent to us, and you can remove it any time with “Clear recent”.

subsections.title: 3.2 Metadata reports
paragraphs: Metadata reports are small records describing the technical properties of a file. By default, a file's metadata report is deleted when the file is deleted, whether you delete it yourself or it is removed at the end of the retention period. The Privacy & data tab of your Account page has a setting that lets you choose to keep metadata reports after their files are gone. Visitors without an account do not have this setting: their metadata reports are always deleted together with their files.

subsections.title: 3.3 Deleting your files
paragraphs: If you have an account, you can delete an individual result, Darkroom project, Motion project or Aperture project, delete all of your files at once, or delete your whole account from the Account page. Visitors without an account can delete their own results during the session in which they were created.

subsections.title: 3.4 Deleting your account
paragraphs: When you delete your account from the Account page, we:
bullets: cancel your Premium or Pro subscription with Stripe, if you have one;
delete your files, your Darkroom, Motion and Aperture projects and your saved voices;
delete your account record and settings and detach your remaining activity records from your identity;
ask our first-party analytics to delete the analytics data linked to your account (see Section 6);
delete your sign-in login.
afterBullets: For 30 days afterwards we keep a minimal deletion record that contains only a one-way hash of your account identifier and the deletion date. It exists so that nothing from the deleted account can be attached to a new sign-up, and it is then purged automatically. Records held by Stripe are governed by Stripe's own policies. If any step cannot be completed, the Account page tells you, and you can contact us at the address in Section 16.

subsections.title: 3.5 Exporting your data
paragraphs: Signed-in users can download an export of their data from the Account page. It is a ZIP file containing your history, projects, saved voices (without their audio), file list, account details and metadata reports. It does not contain the media files themselves, so download those before they expire. Exports are limited to a small number of requests per hour.

subsections.title: 3.6 Other records
paragraphs: We may retain limited technical logs, security records, abuse-prevention records, analytics records, or legal compliance records for longer where reasonably necessary to operate the service, protect against abuse, enforce our policies, comply with law, resolve disputes, or maintain security. These records are not intended to preserve full uploaded media files after their retention period ends. Analytics data follows the periods in Section 6.3.

sections.title: 4. AI Processing
paragraphs: Some Media Manipulator features may use automated systems or AI-assisted tools to process uploaded media, metadata, audio, video, text, transcripts, captions, descriptions, summaries, or other content.
AI-assisted features may be used to:
bullets: transcribe audio or video;
generate captions;
summarize content;
describe images, videos, or audio;
classify content for safety or brand-suitability;
detect suspected illegal, prohibited, abusive, adult, violent, graphic, or otherwise advertiser-sensitive content;
help prevent misuse of the service.
afterBullets: All AI processing used by Media Manipulator is performed locally on our own servers or infrastructure that we control. We do not outsource uploaded files, generated outputs, transcripts, summaries, descriptions, or content-safety scans to third-party AI providers for processing.

The AI features use open models and tools that we run ourselves, mainly on a self-hosted GPU server: Whisper for transcription, Real-ESRGAN for image upscaling, rembg and LaMa for selecting a subject and healing spots in photos, Demucs for separating audio, Chatterbox and Qwen3-TTS for voice cloning, voice design and speech, and other local models, plus language and vision models served through Ollama for text tasks such as summaries, descriptions and caption translation.

This means that when AI features are used, your uploaded files and generated outputs remain within Media Manipulator’s processing environment and are handled according to the storage, retention, deletion, and security practices described in this Privacy Policy.

Uploaded files and generated outputs are kept and deleted as described in Section 3, including when AI features are used. After the applicable retention period they are deleted from our active systems unless earlier deletion occurs or limited retention is legally required for security, abuse prevention, legal compliance, or enforcement purposes.
AI-generated outputs may be imperfect, incomplete, or inaccurate. Users are responsible for reviewing any AI-generated output before relying on it.

We do not use uploaded files to publicly identify users. We do not claim ownership of uploaded files. We do not sell uploaded files or generated outputs. We do not provide uploaded files or generated outputs to third-party AI providers for model training or AI processing.

The one exception is Medi, our AI assistant (Section 1.13): its conversations, and in the editors a short summary of your project and small preview images, are sent to OpenRouter and Anthropic to generate its answers, as described there. Medi never sends your original files, and we never use your files to train a model.

sections.title: 5. Advertising
paragraphs: Media Manipulator may display advertisements, including advertisements served by Google AdSense or other advertising partners.

Advertising is limited and may change. We show ads only on selected tool pages, never on our home, pricing, account or legal pages, and Premium and Pro subscribers do not see ads. Ads appear only when advertising is switched on for the site, and Google's ad script loads on pages that can show ads, with all consent signals denied until you choose; it serves non-personalised ads until then. Google's consent signals for advertising are denied by default and are updated according to your choice in “Cookie settings” in the footer.

Third-party vendors, including Google, may use cookies to serve ads based on a user’s prior visits to Media Manipulator or other websites. Google’s use of advertising cookies enables it and its partners to serve ads to users based on their visit to Media Manipulator and/or other sites on the Internet.

Users may opt out of personalized advertising by visiting Google’s Ads Settings. Users may also opt out of some third-party vendors’ use of cookies for personalized advertising by visiting industry opt-out pages where available.
Advertising partners may collect or receive information from our website and other websites and use that information to provide measurement services and targeted ads.
We do not control third-party advertising cookies or tracking technologies. Their use is governed by the privacy policies of the third parties that provide them.

subsections.title: 5.1 Advertising cookies and Google AdSense
paragraphs: Google, as a third-party vendor, uses cookies to serve ads on Media Manipulator through Google AdSense. Google’s use of the DoubleClick cookie and its other advertising cookies enables it and its partners to serve ads to you based on your visits to Media Manipulator and/or other sites on the Internet. The cookies and identifiers involved are listed in Section 1.5.

Non-personalised ads: Google’s consent signals for advertising start as denied for every visitor, so until you allow advertising Google serves only non-personalised ads. These are not based on your past browsing; they are chosen from the page you are viewing and your general location (no more precise than your city), and where storage is allowed Google may still use cookies or identifiers to limit how often you see the same ad (frequency capping), for aggregated ad reporting and to prevent fraud and abuse. In the EEA, the UK and Switzerland, if you do not consent, Google serves limited ads, which use no cookies or local storage for advertising.

Consent in the EEA, the UK and Switzerland: visitors there see Google’s own consent message, a Google-certified consent management platform that uses the IAB Transparency and Consent Framework (TCF) v2.2, which asks whether Google and its advertising partners may use cookies and personal data for ads. Our own cookie bar asks about our first-party analytics only. You can reopen either one and change or withdraw your choice at any time from “Cookie settings” in the footer. Elsewhere, advertising follows your choice in “Cookie settings”, and a Global Privacy Control signal or “Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information” always refuses personalised advertising (see Section 14).
You can opt out of personalised advertising, or learn more, here:
bullets: Google Ads Settings, to turn off personalised ads from Google: https://adssettings.google.com
the Digital Advertising Alliance’s WebChoices tool, to opt out of personalised ads from participating third-party vendors: https://www.aboutads.info/choices
Your Online Choices, for visitors in the European Union: https://youronlinechoices.eu
Google’s page “How Google uses information from sites or apps that use our services”: https://policies.google.com/technologies/partner-sites
afterBullets: Who sees ads: only visitors who are not signed in and free accounts. Premium and Pro subscribers never see ads, and no ad units are placed on their pages.
Our ads.txt file, which lists the companies authorised to sell ad space on Media Manipulator (only Google), is public at https://www.media-manipulator.com/ads.txt.

sections.title: 6. Analytics
paragraphs: Media Manipulator uses its own first-party analytics, built and operated by us and hosted on our own infrastructure at analytics.media-manipulator.com. It is the primary way we understand which tools are used, where they fail, and what to build next.

We previously used Mixpanel and Firebase Analytics. Both have been removed, as has Firebase Performance monitoring. Firebase is used for account sign-in and, in the mobile app only, for push notifications (Firebase Cloud Messaging) and crash reports (Firebase Crashlytics) — see Section 17.

subsections.title: 6.1 What our analytics collects
paragraphs: When you have consented to analytics, we record events such as:
bullets: pages viewed and how long you were actively engaged with them;
which tool you used, and the outcome — file selected, upload started or failed, job started, completed or failed, result previewed, download started or completed;
the file extension, file size, and media kind of the file you processed;
the tool settings you chose, recorded as preset values or ranges rather than free text;
account events: an account was created, signed in to, or signed out of;
page performance measurements (Core Web Vitals) and client-side errors;
your device type, browser and version, operating system, viewport size, language, and time zone;
the referring website and any campaign parameters in the link you arrived through;
your country, region, and city, derived from your IP address;
your account tier at the time of each event.
afterBullets: Each event carries an anonymous device identifier and a visit identifier so that a sequence of actions can be understood as one visit. If you are signed in, events are also associated with your account.

subsections.title: 6.2 What our analytics never collects
paragraphs: These are technical guarantees enforced in our code, not just policy:
bullets: We do not store your IP address on analytics events. Your IP is used in memory to derive an approximate location and network operator, and is then discarded before the event is recorded.
We do not collect file names. Only the file extension is recorded.
We do not collect the contents of your files, transcripts, captions, summaries, or any AI-generated output.
We do not collect email addresses in event data. Anything resembling an email address is automatically removed, both in your browser and again on our server.

Our first-party analytics does not use cookies. Its identifiers are stored in your browser’s local storage, and our analytics endpoint is configured so that your browser cannot send cookies to it at all. Google Analytics 4 (Section 6.4) is separate and, if you allow analytics, may set its own cookies.
We do not sell your analytics data. The only analytics data that leaves our systems is the three Google Analytics 4 events described in Section 6.4, subject to your analytics choice.

subsections.title: 6.3 How long we keep it
bullets: Individual events and visit records: 13 months, after which they are deleted automatically.
Device and account records: deleted after 25 months without activity.
Records of your consent choices: 5 years, because we are required to be able to demonstrate what you agreed to and when.
Aggregated daily statistics, which contain no identifiers and describe no individual: kept indefinitely.

subsections.title: 6.4 Google Analytics 4
paragraphs: We keep a deliberately minimal Google Analytics 4 configuration as an independent cross-check on our own numbers. Google's analytics script is loaded only after you consent to analytics, and nothing is sent to Google before that: no script request, no events, and no IP address or browser details. Once you consent, exactly three events are sent to Google: a page view (with the page address and title), an account sign-up (with the sign-up method), and a completed job (with the tool name and media type). Nothing else is forwarded, and events from before you consented are not sent. If you withdraw consent, we stop sending events to Google. Once allowed, Google receives the technical data that any web request involves, such as your IP address and browser details, and may set its own cookies.

subsections.title: 6.5 If you decline analytics
paragraphs: If you decline, we record no events about you at all. We keep a single count of how many times each page was viewed, broken down by country and date, with no identifier of any kind attached — individually or in combination, a row in that count cannot be traced to a person, a device, or a visit. It exists so that a change in how many people decline cannot be mistaken for a change in how many people visit.

subsections.title: 6.6 Identifiers we use regardless of your choice
paragraphs: The anonymous device and visit identifiers described above are created whether or not you consent to analytics, because our API needs them to enforce free-tier limits and to block abuse. That is a strictly necessary purpose and is not analytics: without them we could not offer the tools without an account. What your consent controls is whether we record behavioural events against those identifiers.

sections.title: 7. Legal Basis for Processing
paragraphs: Depending on where you are located, we may process personal information based on one or more legal bases, including:
bullets: providing the service requested by the user;
our legitimate interests in operating, securing, improving, and monetizing the website;
compliance with legal obligations;
user consent where required, including for certain cookies, analytics, personalized advertising, or AI-related processing.
afterBullets: For first-party analytics specifically: in the EEA, the UK and Switzerland we rely on your consent and collect nothing until you have given it. In the United States we rely on notice and your right to opt out, which is available at any time from the footer. Where we cannot determine your location, we treat you as requiring consent.

The anonymous device and visit identifiers used to enforce free-tier limits and prevent abuse rely on our legitimate interest in operating and securing the service, and on providing the service you requested. Records of your consent choices are kept to comply with a legal obligation to be able to demonstrate them.

sections.title: 8. Sharing Information
paragraphs: We may share information with:
bullets: hosting and cloud infrastructure providers;
Amazon Web Services, which hosts our file storage (Amazon S3, region us-west-2);

Google, for Firebase Authentication (sign-in), the limited Google Analytics 4 events described in Section 6.4, Firebase Cloud Messaging and Firebase Crashlytics for the mobile app (Section 17) and, where ads are shown, Google AdSense;
Apple, when you choose Sign in with Apple (Apple verifies your sign-in; we receive the name and email address or relay address you allow);
advertising partners;
security, abuse-detection, and content-safety providers;

AI processing is performed locally on our own servers or infrastructure that we control, and we do not share uploaded files, generated outputs, transcripts, summaries, descriptions, or content-safety scans with third-party AI providers for AI processing;
OpenRouter, Inc. and Anthropic, to generate Medi's answers (Section 1.13): your messages, the page you are on, and in the editors a summary of your project and small preview images;
Stripe, our payment processor, when you subscribe to Premium or Pro (we do not receive or store your card number);
law enforcement, regulators, or authorities when required by law or when necessary to report suspected illegal content;
professional advisors, such as attorneys, accountants, or security consultants;
business successors in the event of a merger, acquisition, financing, reorganization, or sale of assets.
afterBullets: We do not sell uploaded files.
Translators we hire submit their work as GitHub pull requests made by CreaTV Ltd.'s GitHub App; those submissions contain only translation text, no personal data about visitors.

sections.title: 9. User Responsibilities
paragraphs: Users are responsible for the content they upload, process, convert, edit, transcribe, summarize, or download through Media Manipulator.
Users must not upload content that:
bullets: they do not own or have permission to process;
infringes copyrights, trademarks, privacy rights, publicity rights, or other legal rights;
contains child sexual abuse material or exploitation;
contains malware, viruses, or harmful code;
is illegal to possess, process, upload, distribute, or transmit;
violates our Terms of Service or Acceptable Use rules.
afterBullets: Use of Media Manipulator does not transfer ownership of uploaded content to us.

sections.title: 10. Security
paragraphs: We use reasonable technical and organizational measures designed to protect uploaded files, generated outputs, logs, and other information from unauthorized access, misuse, loss, or disclosure.

However, no online service, storage system, or transmission method is completely secure. Users should avoid uploading highly sensitive, confidential, or legally restricted content unless they understand and accept the risks.

sections.title: 11. Children’s Privacy
paragraphs: Media Manipulator is not intended for children under the age of 13, or the minimum age required by applicable law in the user’s jurisdiction.
We do not knowingly collect personal information from children. If we learn that we have collected personal information from a child without appropriate consent, we will take steps to delete it.

sections.title: 12. International Users
paragraphs: Media Manipulator may be operated from the United States or other locations. If you access the website from outside the United States, your information may be processed in countries that may have different data protection laws than your country of residence.
By using Media Manipulator, you understand that your information may be transferred to and processed in the United States or other jurisdictions.

sections.title: 13. Your Choices and Rights
paragraphs: Depending on your location, you may have rights regarding your personal information, such as the right to:
bullets: request access to personal information we maintain about you;
request correction or deletion;
object to or restrict certain processing;
withdraw consent where processing is based on consent;
opt out of certain advertising or analytics technologies;
request a copy of your information.
afterBullets: You can change your analytics choice at any time from “Cookie settings” in the footer. If you are in the United States, “Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information” in the footer opts you out of any sharing for advertising purposes.

You can export or delete your analytics data yourself, immediately, from “Cookie settings” in the footer under “Your data”. Export downloads a complete copy of what our analytics holds about you as a file; Delete permanently erases your analytics history and gives your browser a brand-new anonymous ID. If you are signed in, both cover every device linked to your account. Because these tools act immediately, they satisfy the response periods the applicable law allows (30 days under CPRA, one month under the GDPR) by construction. You can also email us using the details below and we will do the same on your behalf within those periods.

One category of records survives deletion: the log of your own consent and opt-out choices. Laws that let you delete your data also require us to be able to prove how we handled your choices (GDPR Article 17(3)(b)), so those records are kept for five years and then deleted. They contain your choices and when you made them — not your browsing activity.

If you have an account, you can delete individual files, delete all of your files, export your data as a ZIP file, sign out of all devices, or delete your account yourself from the Account page (see Section 3).
Once a file has been deleted, whether by you or at the end of its retention period, we cannot retrieve it or provide access to it.

sections.title: 14. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control
paragraphs: Media Manipulator honours Global Privacy Control (GPC). If your browser or an extension sends a GPC signal, we automatically treat it as an opt-out of any sale or sharing of your personal information for advertising purposes, we apply it on every visit — including overriding an advertising opt-in you may have given previously — and we record that we did so.

GPC is an opt-out of sale and sharing. It does not switch off our first-party analytics, because analytics we run on our own domain for our own product decisions is neither a sale nor a share. Analytics is a separate choice, available at any time from “Cookie settings” in the footer.

We do not respond to the older “Do Not Track” browser signal. No standard was ever agreed for how sites should interpret it and no regulator gave it legal effect; GPC is the signal that carries weight, and it is the one we honour.

sections.title: 15. Changes to This Privacy Policy
paragraphs: We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. When we make changes, we will update the “Last Updated” date at the top of this page.
If we make material changes, we may provide additional notice, such as by posting a notice on the website.
Your continued use of Media Manipulator after changes are posted means you accept the updated Privacy Policy.

sections.title: 16. Contact Us
paragraphs: The contact form at media-manipulator.com/contact reaches the same people as the address below; Section 1.11 explains what it collects and how long messages are kept.
If you have questions about this Privacy Policy or how Media Manipulator handles information, contact us at:

sections.title: 17. The Media Manipulator App
paragraphs: This section applies to the Media Manipulator app for Android, operated by CreaTV Ltd. It adds to the rest of this Privacy Policy, which also applies: the app uses the same account, the same servers and the same retention settings as the website. To use the app you sign in to your Media Manipulator account.

subsections.title: 17.1 What the app collects
paragraphs: When you use the app, we and our providers receive:
bullets: your account data, as described in Section 1.7;

pricing.subtitle: Every plan runs the same tools on the same hardware. What changes is how much you can put through them in a day.

faq.q1: What counts toward my daily allowance?
faq.a1: Each plan has two separate daily allowances that add up. An everyday job is one conversion, compression, transcode or other standard tool. An AI job is one run of a tool that uses an AI model, such as transcription, upscaling or vocal removal. An AI job never uses up an everyday job, so you can use every AI job and still have every everyday job. Darkroom exports have their own allowance. Previews, probes and downloads are free — you are only charged for work the server actually does.
faq.q2: What happens when I run out?
faq.a2: Nothing breaks. The tool tells you the allowance is spent and offers the next tier up. Your allowance resets at midnight UTC.
faq.a3: Yes. Ads pay for the free tier, so only Premium and Pro remove them. There are never more than two ads on a page, never over the tools, and never on the home, pricing, account or legal pages. There are no interstitials, countdowns or forced waits on any plan.
faq.q4: Can I use it without an account at all?
faq.a4: Yes, and that is deliberate. Every tool works signed out — an account just raises the ceiling and keeps your history. Without an account your files are kept for 24 hours; with an account you choose how long, from 24 hours to 2 years.
faq.a5: Editing in {{brand}} is free: previews, every adjustment, masks, looks and undo cost nothing. Each export counts as one everyday job, selecting a subject with AI counts as one everyday job (repeating the same request is free), and each time you press Heal counts as one AI job. whatYouCanDo.title: Tools for every kind of media file
whatYouCanDo.video: Video. Compress a video for email or the web, trim it to the part you need with a fast cut that keeps the original quality, turn a short clip into an animated GIF, or package it as HLS for adaptive streaming. Large uploads go straight to our storage, so long recordings work too.
whatYouCanDo.images: Images and PDFs. Remove EXIF metadata such as GPS location before you share a photo, compress an image for a faster page, resize it to exact pixel dimensions, and convert images to PDF or PDF pages to JPG.
whatYouCanDo.audio: Audio and speech. Extract the audio track from a video as MP3, WAV, M4A, FLAC or OGG, and transcribe what is said into searchable text or captions. Transcription runs Whisper on our own GPU server.
whatYouCanDo.ai: AI tools. Remove the background from a photo, restore and upscale an old picture, compare video restoration models side by side on a short clip, or turn scanned pages into a searchable PDF. Every model runs on servers we operate.
whatYouCanDo.editors: Editors. When one conversion is not enough, Darkroom is a multi-track video editor and Motion animates SVG artwork on a keyframe timeline, and Aperture edits photos with adjustment layers and masks. All three run in your browser, and signing in keeps your projects with your account.

whatWeDont.title: The things we leave out on purpose
items: No third-party AI. Your files are never sent to an outside AI provider. Transcription, background removal, upscaling and every other AI tool run on our own GPU server.

No watermarks on your files. Converted images, videos, audio and documents come back without a logo or a mark. The one exception is synthetic speech from the voice tools, which carries an inaudible marker that identifies it as AI-generated.

No account needed for most tools. Conversion, compression, trimming and metadata removal work without signing up. A free account adds a larger daily allowance, saved projects and control over how long your files are kept.
No files kept longer than you choose. Files are kept 24 hours for guests; with a free account you choose 24 hours to 2 years, and you can delete any file sooner from your account.

contentStudioGuide.whenToUseBody: Reach for Darkroom when one file isn’t enough: combining several clips, adding titles or background music, layering overlays, or trimming and re-ordering footage into a finished video.
contentStudioGuide.supportedMediaBody: Video (MP4, MOV, WebM, MKV), images (JPG, PNG, WebP), and audio (MP3, WAV, AAC). The final export is MP4 (H.264 video, AAC audio).
contentStudioGuide.step1: Create a project and choose a resolution (up to 4K) and frame rate (24/30/60 fps).

contentStudioGuide.step5: Preview the composite, then export to MP4 and download.
contentStudioGuide.timelineBody: The timeline is frame-accurate — the playhead and clip edges snap to the project frame rate. Tracks composite in stacking order, so a clip on a higher track renders over the ones below it. That’s how titles, logos, and picture-in-picture overlays sit on top of your base video.
contentStudioGuide.exportBody: Exporting renders the whole sequence — every track, trim, and overlay — into one downloadable MP4 encoded with H.264 video and AAC audio.
contentStudioGuide.limitationsBody: Darkroom is actively evolving. Core editing — multi-track timeline, trim/split, layering, audio mixing, and MP4 export — is available now. Advanced effects continue to be added over time.
